en: My mother, sacred as Mecca.
Though I pleaded, they heeded no word.
The days had shriveled me to a handful;
I embraced and kissed my darling,
Breathed once the scent of her breast—
Your venerable white-haired mother.
I tore my hair until it thinned;
Blood streaming from both my eyes
Flowed down over my breast.
I shrieked aloud in grief,
Parted from my own true mother.
As the vile ones beat me,
And subjected me to this disgrace,
I wished to sink into the earth, but it was hard;
I wished to die, but life was sweet.
They caused my darling bitter pain,
They ground me utterly to dust,
And dragged my mother away—
My generous venerable mother,
My broad-hearted dear one.
‘How can I remain alive?’ I cried.
‘From this day on, oh Mother,
Whom shall I hold sacred?’ I cried.
I turned my face toward death
And tore out my disheveled hair.
Because of all that had befallen,
Because of my dear mother,
I raised a piercing cry,
Not sparing my fly-sized soul.
‘Let me depart for the true world;
For my venerable white-haired mother,
I would gladly die contending.’
For six thousand camels and a thousand colts,
The keen Albar sword that was commissioned—
My mother entrusted it to you!
If you bring it back to me,
Bring my venerable white-haired mother
And let my eyes behold her.
Let me gaze upon her face,
Breathe once the scent of her breast,
And only then let me die!
My black crag no goose can circle,
My great mountain left by the departed,
Light of my seeing eyes,
Strength of my heart,
My only son, fare safely.
Your mother has no strength left.
Go in safety and return unharmed;
Do not leave your poor, wretched mother
Longing—come back quickly.
Go safely and return sound.
My orphaned son, if only
Once within seven days
I may safely see your face.
Saying, “My cherished orphan will return,”
I shall grieve for six days;
But if you do not come within six days,
If I do not see your radiant face,
I shall die before death comes.’
Moon-like Aichürök,
For the son she bore at death’s door,
Let her thoughts scatter far and wide.
Amid universal anguish and hardship,
Behold the plight of her only son.
Her heart was deeply troubled,
And tears poured from her eyes.
As though her son would never return,
Aichürök grieved,
Though he was merely setting forth
Upon a campaign.
So great was the poor woman’s anguish,
As though they would never meet again.
The woman screamed and shrieked,
Unable to bear it, she wailed.
There is no end to my misery.
The one who unleashed volleys of fire,
Who rescued us from calamity
More terrible than any battle cry—
My noble son is not here.
The support on which I relied,
The one in whom I placed my hopes,
My valiant son, is not there.
My heart burns; I have no courage left.
The enemy has torn away my wing;
My heart burns beneath the vast blue sky.
Had you been there then, my son,
Would they not have spared my blood?
Would they not have left my herds unscattered?
Would the raging Jediger
Not have spared my life?
Across the lower valley of Talas,
Would they have dared draw their boundary?
Would you not have faced them in battle
And crushed those evildoers?
Yesterday, when the enemy surrounded us,
When our people were left helpless
And suffered bitter torment,
I failed to do what was right—
Curse my womanhood!
I let them seize my livestock,
And let my life become their spoil.
I let them cut down my silken banner,
And let them drag away
The mother granted me by fortune.
If you encounter my mother,
Go and exchange greetings with her;
To be my strength and comfort,
Bring your noble, blessed mother
Back this way with you.
Let my eyes behold her;
Bring me the one I revere above all people—
My son, bring her back to me.
If you abandon her, shame will follow.
My heroic son, heed my words:
If one perishes, does not the black earth
Receive the whole world?
Do not grieve, Mother;
Will the descendant of a heroic khan
Rest before finding his people?
Would God strike down a warrior thus,
Leaving him unable to find his people?
The goshawk flies to its own land;
The forlorn hero returns to his people.
The Telik bird flies to its own land;
The wanderer returns to his people.
I shall go to the dear people
Who sit waiting to cherish me.
I am the khan’s sole descendant;
Why should I keep fleeing?
I shall go to the renowned people
Who wait to place their hopes in me.
I am the son of a noble prince;
Why should I shun my homeland?
There is silver on its sunny slopes,
Upon the rolling ridges of the yellow hills;
I long for my people, and I shall go.
There is gold upon its hills,
Upon the rugged ridges of its rocky mountains;
My thoughts are with my people, and I shall go.’
Saying this, the hero Seytek
Bade farewell to his mother with these words,
And spoke many other wondrous things.
He raised a gold-crescented banner,
Donned armor no bullet could pierce,
And mounted a swift horse no bullet could catch.
The tail of Kylkürөң
He knotted diagonally.
To free-flowing Keng-Kol and broad Talas,
To his homeland went the hero Seytek.
To the dear Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
To his nation went the hero Seytek.
He crossed the mottled rolling ridges,
Traversed mountains with arduous passes,
And journeyed along the road ahead.
Spurring himself on with courage,
He appealed to the spirit
Of his bloodthirsty father-in-law.
Her heart sank and broke apart—
A dreadful sight to behold—
And tears poured from her eyes.
From her quail-like eyes
Separate streams of tears flowed;
From her blackcurrant-dark eyes
Tears fell a whip’s length.
Unable to draw back the mucus from her nose,
Unable to wipe the tears from her eyes,
She stood weeping and shrieking,
Thinking thoughts she could not restrain,
Pondering the child’s fate without answer.
Tormented and burning with grief,
She wondered, ‘My only son has never seen this road;
What will become of him?’
His dear mother stood grieving.
As his mother stood thus,
The hero Seytek grew fierce,
Angrily making ready.
Wisdom came to him from the unseen;
Murmuring with gathering resolve,
This poor heroic son
Spoke to his mother:
‘Alas, Mother, what are you saying?
Does a mortal man not die?
Whatever command God ordains,
Must not a mortal servant endure it?
Does one whose time has come not die?
When the angel reaches out five fingers,
Saying, “We have need of this mortal,”
And the command has been given,
The nimble tongue is stilled from speaking.
When the naked blade of Gabriel
Comes rushing straight against him,
When five fingers reach out,
When the soul departs and a person dies,
Will the dug grave not receive him?
Almighty God creates living souls
In every different form.
The valleys stretch broad and level,
The wooded mountains rise in grandeur;
Our wondrous Talas
Has snow upon its encircling peaks,
And every kind of living creature.
All creatures endowed with life
Are gathered here in abundance.
Cuckoos sing upon the hills,
And nightingales in the woods
Pour forth their many plaintive songs.
When the mournful nightingale sings,
Those who bear sorrow long to listen;
Many a melancholy soul
Yearns to enter its delight.
Willows bend low,
Argali cluster on the hills.
Deer shelter among the knolls,
And there, upon the terraces, wild goats
Pour across in every direction.
Their ears held sharply upright,
Wolves prowl along the lower slopes.
Their tails trailing behind them,
Foxes frolic on the plain.
Swift bustards and great bustards
Scatter to graze upon the hills;
Every blessing is true delight,
And white waters pour from the uplands.
Our wondrous, spacious Talas,
Its apples are as large as horses’ heads,
Its walnuts like stones in a stream;
Feather grass sways waist-high,
Tulips and sorrel
Twist and trail about the waist.
From the broad, branching valleys
Springs divide and flow.
Perhaps in wonder at Talas,
The boy’s thoughts wandered away.
When he looked closely upon broad Talas,
He rode on without sparing his horse,
Never halting to rest his steed,
Never lying down to satisfy his sleep,
Never leaning on an elbow to rest,
Never dozing even for a moment;
He hurried on in high excitement,
Roused like a lion,
Travelling without pause,
Riding onward without restraint.
How could the hero have foreseen
The mist lying like the back of a saddle?
He made his way toward the haze.
On this side of the mist
Was a valley of surpassing cliffs.
Kara-Buura and great Chatkal
Form a mountain range adjoining Talas;
Its rocky passes are perilously narrow,
Its ridges are sheer precipices,
Its mountains girdle the valley like a rim.
It is called the broad Chatkal range.
He crossed over Chatkal,
And before him lay broad Talas—
